concepts.title: Germ Theory and the Golden Age of Microbiology

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Germ Theory and the Golden Age of Microbiology' refers to.
questions.a: Microbiology grew from Leeuwenhoek's animalcules through Pasteur's swan-necked flasks - which killed spontaneous generation and launched the germ theory of disease - to Koch's pure-culture proof that Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax; the late 1800s and early 1900s became the Golden Age, as solid media, Petri's 1887 dish, selective media of the early twentieth century and antibiotic-era medicine turned microbes into laboratory objects and living factories.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Germ Theory and the Golden Age of Microbiology'.
questions.a: Broth spoiled only when dust reached it, so microbes come from microbes - and that insight built pure culture, sterilisation and medical microbiology.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Germ Theory and the Golden Age of Microbiology' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Nutritional Categories of Microbes' refers to.
questions.a: Microbes sort by where carbon and energy come from: heterotrophs feed on organic molecules, autotrophs fix carbon dioxide; chemoautotrophs oxidise sulphur or nitrite for both needs while photoautotrophs harvest light, chemoheterotrophs burn organic nutrients, and photoheterotrophs such as green and purple non-sulphur bacteria mix light energy with organic carbon - with lithotrophs and organotrophs naming the electron sources.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nutritional Categories of Microbes'.
questions.a: Two questions classify any microbe - where does its carbon come from and where does its energy come from.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Nutritional Categories of Microbes' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Pure Culture Techniques' refers to.
questions.a: A pure culture holds one strain alone, won by dilution on solid media: the streak plate thins a loopful across an agar surface until isolated colonies appear, the pour plate mixes one-millilitre aliquots of serially diluted sample into melted agar before it sets, and the spread plate distributes a tenth-millilitre drop with a sterile L-shaped rod - colonies arise because daughters stay put where their parent landed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pure Culture Techniques'.
questions.a: Dilute until single cells land apart; each colony is then a clone you can pick.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pure Culture Techniques' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Factors Affecting Microbial Growth' refers to.
questions.a: Growth bends to its surroundings: mesophiles peak between twenty and forty-five degrees while thermophiles push toward fifty to sixty-five and extreme thermophiles survive past one hundred, most microbes favour neutral pH though fungi prefer slight acidity, and oxygen tolerance splits obligate aerobes, obligate and aerotolerant anaerobes and facultative species, with carbon dioxide and correct light wavelengths completing the checklist for autotrophs and phototrophs.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Factors Affecting Microbial Growth'.
questions.a: Fix temperature, pH, oxygen, carbon dioxide and light to the organism's habit before expecting growth.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Factors Affecting Microbial Growth' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'The Bacterial Growth Curve Phases' refers to.
questions.a: Plotting log of viable cells against time reveals four acts: a lag phase where cells build division machinery without multiplying, the exponential or log phase of maximal constant-rate doubling when cultures are chemically most uniform, a stationary phase balancing births against deaths as nutrients thin and wastes mount, and a decline phase of logarithmic death - the shape lactic-acid Streptococci write into their own medium as acidity rises.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Bacterial Growth Curve Phases'.
questions.a: Flat, climb, plateau, fall - each phase reflects a different balance between building cells and killing them.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Bacterial Growth Curve Phases' taught, and from which source text?
